chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated to us, from his father, from Al-Nufali, from Al-Sakuni, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon them), who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Three [people] — I do not know which of them is greater in sin: The one who walks with the funeral procession without a cloak (or shroud), The one who says: 'Be gentle with him,' And the one who says: 'Seek forgiveness for him, may God forgive you.'
ai.seo_question: What are the three sins associated with walking in a funeral procession according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal*, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) identified three specific behaviors during funeral processions as grave sins, expressing uncertainty regarding which was the most severe. These offenses include walking without a cloak (indicating lack of reverence or modesty), advising mourners to 'be gentle' with the deceased (potentially implying undue attachment or lack of acceptance of death), and invoking forgiveness for the deceased (which may imply doubt about their status). This highlights the Shia emphasis on proper etiquette (adab) and theological precision in funeral rites.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 3-266 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim quoted Al-Nawfaly, on the authority of Al-Sakoony, on the authority of Ja’far ibn Muhammad (MGB) , on the authority of his father (MGB) , on the authority of his forefathers (MGB), on the authority of Ali (MGB) that God’s Prophet (MGB) said, “Of the following three I do not really know which one is a greater offense than the others.

The first is following a funeral procession without one’s robe. The second is saying ‘be benign to him.’ And the third one is saying ‘Seek God’s forgiveness for him. May God forgive you. (when attending a funeral procession).’”
